card.name: Monkey
card.tagline: An energetic 1963 American novelty craze inspired by the Twist and fueled by R&B hits.
card.profile: The monkey is an American novelty fad dance that emerged in the wake of the Twist, reaching its peak popularity in 1963. Driven by Top 10 R&B hits by Major Lance and the Miracles, the dance quickly spread into national youth culture. Although its exact technical movement patterns are unrecorded in the primary sources, it belongs to the early 1960s family of individual novelty dances. It later survived as a nostalgic pop-culture motif across late-twentieth-century television and music.
card.insight: Riding the wave of the Twist, the monkey became a nationwide American novelty craze in the summer of 1963.
card.profile_long:
The monkey emerged during the golden age of American novelty dance crazes in the early 1960s. After the Twist transformed popular social dance between 1959 and the early sixties, it paved the way for an entire wave of solo-oriented dance crazes across the United States. Following the massive success of records by artists like Chubby Checker, young dancers eagerly embraced novelty movements that were dynamic, fun, and easy to perform without traditional ballroom partnering.

In the summer of 1963, the monkey reached the height of its popularity, directly propelled by two major rhythm and blues singles. Chicago artist Major Lance scored a Top 10 hit with 'The Monkey Time', while the Miracles found immense success with 'Mickey's Monkey'. The latter track presented a humorous narrative about William 'Mickey' Stevenson spreading a brand-new dance out of town, helping solidify the dance as an inescapable phenomenon among American teenagers. Along with related novelty crazes of the era such as the Jerk, the Pony, the Watusi, the Mashed Potato, and the Funky Chicken, the monkey became a defining sound and movement of early 1960s youth culture.

Although specific footwork mechanics, hand gestures, and body postures for the monkey are not documented in the historical texts supplied, the dance shared the energetic, independent format popularized by the Twist. Rather than maintaining closed physical contact, dancers moved in parallel to upbeat 1960s pop and soul grooves. The social environment was centered around television dance shows, radio play, teenage hangouts, and commercial record singles, forming a lively youth-driven atmosphere.

Over subsequent decades, the monkey transitioned from a contemporary dance trend into an enduring cultural reference. It appeared frequently across popular media, notably cited in the animated series Johnny Bravo, recurring jokes in The Simpsons, and Japanese anime such as Overman King Gainer. The thrash metal group Exodus also nodded to the craze in their 1989 track 'The Toxic Waltz', reflecting on how performing the monkey had shifted from a ubiquitous teenage trend into a humorous relic of mid-century pop history.

sections.origins_and_history: The monkey emerged as a novelty fad dance in the United States following the global breakthrough of the Twist in the late 1950s and early 1960s. Wikidata dates the dance's inception to circa 1960, listing it as inspired by the Twist. It reached its peak national popularity during the summer of 1963.
sections.how_it_is_danced: Technique not described in sources. The dance is historically categorized alongside the Twist and similar novelty crazes where dancers danced individually without physical contact.
sections.music_and_instruments: The dance was popularized by rhythm and blues and pop singles in 1963, notably Major Lance's 'The Monkey Time' and the Miracles' 'Mickey's Monkey'. Both songs reached the pop Top 10 during the summer of 1963.
sections.costume_and_setting: Not described in sources. It thrived in the context of early 1960s American teenage music culture, record clubs, radio broadcasts, and social dance spaces.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The monkey functioned as a lighthearted teenage novelty and fad dance, offering youth an accessible, entertaining way to participate in the burgeoning R&B and rock and roll dance craze boom of the early 1960s.
sections.notable_figures: Major Lance and the Miracles were central to popularizing the dance through their 1963 hit records. The Miracles' song 'Mickey's Monkey' credited the spread of the dance to William 'Mickey' Stevenson.
sections.lineage: The monkey is an offshoot of the broader early-1960s dance craze wave initiated by the Twist, existing alongside peers like the Jerk, the Pony, the Watusi, the Mashed Potato, and the Funky Chicken.

claims.text: The monkey was a novelty dance that was most popular in 1963.
The Twist inspired a wave of dances including the Jerk, Pony, Watusi, Mashed Potato, Monkey, and Funky Chicken.
The monkey was popularized by two Top 10 pop hits released during the summer of 1963.
The Miracles' hit told a comical story about Mickey Stevenson spreading the new dance.
Thrash metal band Exodus referenced the dance in their song 'The Toxic Waltz'.
The monkey is referenced in the theme song and episodes of the animated comedy series Johnny Bravo.
Wikidata records the inception of the monkey dance to 1960 and notes it was inspired by the Twist.

episode_brief.title_hook: Summer of '63: When America Did the Monkey
episode_brief.logline: Explore how two Top 10 R&B records swept the United States in 1963, launching the monkey as one of the definitive fad dances of the Twist era.
beats: 1959: The Twist breaks out, sparking a wave of individual, touchless teenage novelty dances.
Summer 1963: Major Lance releases 'The Monkey Time', storming the American pop charts.
The Miracles record 'Mickey's Monkey', a humorous story song about William 'Mickey' Stevenson spreading the dance.
Teenagers across the country adopt the monkey as a national novelty craze.
The late 20th century: The monkey lives on as a nostalgic pop-culture hallmark in animation and rock lyrics.
